analysis.one_liner: Freezes most class-action lawsuits over illegal referral fees in mortgage deals for nine months.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have paused class actions alleging mortgage kickbacks, never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act makes it illegal for a lender to pay another lender or a mortgage broker a referral fee that inflates a homebuyer's closing costs. This bill would have ordered federal and state courts to stop — until July 1, 1999 — any class action alleging those payments: no class certification, no class-related discovery, no sanctions, and a freeze on cases where a class had already been certified. Individual lawsuits could continue, but class actions are how most borrowers actually recover, because each person's damages are small.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers facing class actions over referral payments — including payments to brokers known as yield spread premiums — would have gotten a nine-month breather: courts could not certify classes, hear discovery on class issues, or keep cases moving where a class had been certified in 1998. The carve-out allowing certification only for settlements would have made it easier for defendants to negotiate industry-friendly global settlements during the freeze.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars courts from certifying classes, ordering class-related discovery, or imposing sanctions in any RESPA case alleging a payment from one lender to another lender or to a mortgage broker, until July 1, 1999.
It orders a stay of any such class action where a class had been certified on or after January 1, 1998, halting those proceedings for the duration.
It leaves individual (non-class) RESPA suits untouched, so lenders would still face single-borrower claims, but not the collective actions that aggregate small damages into significant recoveries.

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers with pending or potential class claims over inflated settlement charges would lose their main enforcement vehicle while the freeze ran, and any recovery would be delayed or channeled into settlements negotiated while plaintiffs' leverage was suspended.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argued in this era that RESPA's ban on 'things of value' had been stretched to cover routine broker compensation, exposing standard industry practice to enormous retroactive class liability; a moratorium gave courts, HUD, and Congress time to sort out the rules. The bill's defenders could also point out that it preserved individual suits and allowed class certification for settlement purposes.

The settlement carve-out cuts both ways: while it lets defendants resolve cases, certification 'directly in connection with the settlement' is the tool courts use to approve industry-wide deals, so the freeze could have pushed borrowers toward settlement terms negotiated while their cases were otherwise locked in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the mortgage industry, the cost of the bill was low — a time-limited procedural pause — and the benefit was large: it defused a wave of class actions. For homebuyers, the cost was real: class actions are the practical remedy for referral-fee overcharges, since individual RESPA recoveries are small, and the bill paused that remedy without any offsetting protection. The bill offered nothing to borrowers in exchange for the freeze.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1998 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee in October; the Congress ended in January 1999 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Rod Grams introduced the bill on June 25, 1998, with 18 original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
On October 13, 1998, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Oversight and Courts, where it sat.
No further action was taken before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the moratorium never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuyers and plaintiffs' lawyers pursuing class actions over mortgage referral fees — the freeze they were fighting never happened, and lenders and brokers got no litigation reprieve.

for.name: Sen. Rod Grams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its cosponsorship drive.

for.name: 12 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors, including Sens. Faircloth, Thurmond, Brownback, Ashcroft, Mack, McCain, and Enzi.

for.name: 6 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors, including Sens. Breaux, Akaka, Inouye, Reid, Bryan, and Bennett (I/D).

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: His committee never took up the bill — no hearing or markup is recorded — and it stalled at the subcommittee level.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors signed on the day of introduction — 12 Republicans and 6 Democrats — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: Lenders were the defendants in RESPA class actions alleging they paid referral fees or yield spread premiums to other lenders and brokers, inflating borrowers' closing costs. The bill would have frozen those suits — no class certification, no class discovery, no sanctions — for nine months. It died, so the industry never got the reprieve.

Brokers received the disputed referral payments and were co-defendants in the same class actions; the moratorium covered any case alleging a payment 'by a lender to another lender or to a mortgage broker.' Because the bill died, suits naming brokers could proceed.
